διηγήσασθαι, τότε τὴν ἀναίσχυντον ἐπιφέρει συμβουλήν. Καὶ οὐδὲ αὐ τῷ φανερῶς
εἶπε, Βλασφήμησον. Οἱ γὰρ πονηρὰ συμ βουλεύοντες οὐ τολμῶσιν
ἀνακεκαλυμμένην εἰσά γειν τὴν συμβουλήν. Τί λέγεις, ὦ γύναι; ∆έον ἐξι λεώσασθαι,
δέον καταλλάξαι, παροξῦναι μᾶλλον παρ αινεῖς; Εἰ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς ταῦτα ἐποίησε,
παρακαλέσαι αὐτὸν, οὐ βλασφημῆσαι δεῖ. Πόθεν δὲ δῆλον, ὅτι καὶ ἐρώμενον
τελευτήσω; Πλὴν ὅρα ὅπως εἶχε περὶ τῆς βλασφημίας ἡ γυνή. Ὥσπερ παραχρῆμα
αὐτὴν θάνατον ἐπάγειν ἱκανὴν ἡγεῖτο. Στ. ιʹ. Εἰ τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐδεξάμεθα ἐκ χειρὸς Κυ
ρίου, τὰ κακὰ οὐχ ὑποίσομεν; Ὁ γὰρ μακάριος οὗτος, πανταχόθεν βαλλόμενος,
ἀσφαλέστερον ἵστατο, καὶ μυρία βέλη δεχόμενος, οὐκ ἐνεδίδου. Ἀλλ' ἐκένωσε μὲν
τοῦ διαβόλου τὴν βελοθή κην, αὐτὸς δὲ οὐ κατέπεσεν, οὐδὲ ὑπεσκελίσθη. Ἀλλ'
ὥσπερ ἄριστος κυβερνήτης, οὔτε μαινομένης τῆς θα λάσσης, καὶ τῶν κυμάτων
διεγειρομένων κατεποντί ζετο, οὔτε γαλήνης οὔσης ῥᾳθυμότερος ἐγίνετο. Ἀλλ' ἐν
ἑκατέρᾳ τῇ τῶν καιρῶν διαφορᾷ ἴσην τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τέχνην διετήρησε. Καὶ οὔτε
πλοῦτος ἑαυτὸν ἐφύ σησεν, οὔτε πενία ἐταπείνωσεν, οὔτε, κατὰ ῥοῦν τῶν
πραγμάτων φερομένων, ὕπτιος ἦν καὶ ἀναπεπτωκὼς, οὔτε, ὅλης σχεδὸν τῆς οἰκείας
ἀνατραπείσης, καὶ πανολεθρίας γενομένης, διεταράχθη, καὶ τὴν ἀνδρίαν ἤλεγξε τὴν
ἑαυτοῦ. Ἀκουέτωσαν πλούσιοι, ἀκουέτω σαν πένητες· ἑκατέροις γὰρ τὸ διήγημα
χρήσιμον, καὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις ἡ ἱστορία λυσιτελής· καὶ τοῖς ἐν εὐημερίᾳ, καὶ τοῖς
ἐν συμφοραῖς. Ἑκάτερα γὰρ τὰ ὅπλα μεταχειρίσας ὁ τῆς εὐσεβείας ἀγωνιστὴς, ὁ τῆς
οἰκουμένης στεφανίτης, ἐν ἑκατέροις τὸ τρόπαιον ἔστησε· καὶ πρὸς πᾶν εἶδος
πολέμου τοῦ δαίμονος 17.64 ἐπελθόντος ἐκείνου, πρὸς ἅπαντα παρετάξατο, καὶ ἐν
πᾶσιν ἀνεκηρύττετο. Καὶ καθάπερ στρατιώτης γεν ναῖος, καὶ εἰδὼς νυκτομαχεῖν,
τειχομαχεῖν, πεζομα χεῖν, ναυμαχεῖν, καὶ τοξεύειν, καὶ δόρυ σείειν, καὶ σφενδόναις
καὶ ἀκοντίοις, καὶ παντὶ τρόπῳ μάχης περιγίνεσθαι τῆς ἐναντίων καὶ πανταχοῦ κρα
τεῖν· οὕτω δὴ καὶ ὁ γενναῖος ἐκεῖνος ἅπαντα πειρα σμὸν μετὰ πολλῆς ἤνεγκε τῆς
ἀνδρίας, τὸν ἀπὸ πε νίας, τὸν ἀπὸ λιμοῦ, τὸν ἀπὸ νόσου, τὸν ἐξ ὀδύνης, τὸν ἀπὸ
παίδων ἀπωλείας, τὸν ἀπὸ τῶν φίλων, τὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐχθρῶν, τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς γυναικὸς,
τὸν ἀπὸ τῶν οἰκετῶν. Οὐ γὰρ ἦν ἀνθρωπίνη συμφορὰ, ἣ μὴ εἰς τὸ σῶμα ἐξεκενώθη
ἐκείνου. Ἀλλ' ὅμως ἁπάντων ὑπερηνέχθη τῶν δικτύων, καὶ ὑψηλότερος γέγονε τῶν
τοῦ διαβόλου καλάμων. Καὶ τὸ δὴ θαυμαστότερον, ὅτι καὶ πάντα αὐτῷ, καὶ πάντα
μεθ' ὑπερβολῆς, καὶ πάντα ὑφ' ἕν. Μὴ γὰρ τοῦτο ἴδῃς, ὅτι τοσαῦτα ἔπα θεν· ἀλλὰ
πρόσθες, ὅτι οὐδὲ κατὰ μικρὸν, οὐδὲ ἐκ διαστήματος, ἀλλ' ὑφὲν καὶ ὁμοῦ. Οὐ μικρὰ
δὲ αὕτη πειρασμῶν προσθήκη. Τῶν μὲν γὰρ ἄλλων ἕκαστος ἀνθρώπων πρῶτον μὲν
οὐδεὶς ἂν εὑρεθείη πάντα ὑπο μείνας ὁμοῦ, ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ πενίᾳ παλαίει, ὅμως ὑγείας
ἀπολαύει· εἰ δὲ καὶ πενίᾳ καὶ νόσῳ περιεπάρη, ἀλλὰ γυναικὸς πολλάκις ἀπήλαυσε
παραμυθουμένης τὰ δει νὰ, καὶ ἀντὶ λιμένος αὐτῷ γινομένης. Εἰ δὲ μὴ γυναι κὸς
ἀπήλαυσε τοιαύτης, ἀλλ' οὐχ οὕτω συμβουλευ θείσης ὀλέθρια, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ τοὺς
παῖδας ἀθρόον ἀπώλεσεν ἅπαντας· εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀθρόον, ἀλλ' οὐ τοιούτῳ τρόπῳ
τελευτῆς· εἰ δὲ καὶ τοιούτῳ [τρόπῳ] τελευτῆς, ἀλλὰ φίλους ἔσχε παρακαλοῦντας· εἰ
δὲ οὐκ ἔσχε πα ρακαλοῦντας, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ οὕτως ἐπεμβαίνοντας· εἰ δὲ καὶ
ἐπεμβαίνοντας, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ οἰκέτας ὀνειδί ζοντας· εἰ δὲ καὶ ὀνειδίζοντας, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ
καὶ εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἐμπτύοντας· εἰ δὲ καὶ εἰς τὸ πρόσ ωπον ἐμπτύοντας, ἀλλ'
οὐχὶ καὶ νόσῳ τοιαύτῃ περιε πάρει, ἀλλὰ δωματίου καὶ σκέπης ἀπήλαυσε, καὶ οὐκ
ἐπὶ τῆς κοπρίας ἐκάθητο· εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς κοπρίας ἐκάθητο, ἀλλ' ἔσχε τοὺς χεῖρα
ὀρέγοντας· εἰ δὲ μὴ ἔσχε τοὺς χεῖρα ὀρέγοντας, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ ἐπεμβαίνοντας. Οὗτος
δ' ἅπαντα ταῦτα ὑπήνεγκεν. Στίχ. ιαʹ. Παρεγένοντο ἕκαστος ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας χώ ρας πρὸς
αὐτὸν, Ἐλιφὰζ ὁ Θαιμανῶν βασι λεὺς, Βαλδὰδ ὁ Σαυχέων τύραννος, Σωφὰρ
Μιναίων βασιλεύς. Φιλικὴ μὲν ἡ παρουσία σου, φιλικὴ δὲ ἡ παρ αίνεσις. Ἐλιφάζ·
Θεός με διέσπειρεν, ἢ, Θεοῦ μου φαυλισμός. Θαιμὰν, ἔκλειψις αὐτῶν. Σωφὰρ,
σκοπὸς, ἢ φαυλισμός. Βαλδὰδ, παλαίωσις, καὶ ἐπίδοξος. Σαυχαίων, ἀδολεσχία
αὐτῶν. Στίχ. ιαʹ. Ἀκούσαντες δὲ οἱ τρεῖς φίλοι αὐτοῦ τὰ κακὰ πάντα, τὰ ἐπελθόντα
αὐτῷ, παρε γένοντο ἕκαστος ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας χώρας πρὸς αὐτόν. Ἐάν τις ζητῇ, διὰ τί
μετὰ τοσοῦτον χρόνον οἱ φί λοι παραγεγόνασιν, ἐννοείτω πρῶτον μὲν, ὅτι δια
φόρους ᾤκουν χώρας, καὶ μετὰ πλεῖστον χρόνον πολλοὶ μὲν ἤκουσαν ἴσως, τὸ δὲ
pass_a_gloss: ...to narrate, then she brings on the shameless counsel. And she did not even say to him openly, Blaspheme. For those counselling wicked things do not dare to lead in the counsel uncovered. What are you saying, woman? When it is needful to propitiate, when it is needful to reconcile, do you rather advise to provoke? For if God made these things, it is needful to entreat him, not to blaspheme. And from where is it plain that even being loved (printed ἐρώμενον; probably a form of 'saying') I will die? But see how the woman stood about blasphemy: as though she held it sufficient to bring death at once. Verse 10. If we received the good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear the evil things? For this blessed one, being struck from everywhere, was standing more safely, and receiving ten thousand arrows, did not give in. But he emptied the quiver of the devil, and he himself did not fall down, nor was he tripped. But like a best pilot, neither, the sea raging and the waves being stirred up, was he drowned, nor, there being calm, did he become more slack. But in each difference of the seasons he preserved his own art equal. And neither did wealth puff him up, nor poverty humble, nor, the affairs being carried according to the stream, was he lying on his back and reclining, nor, nearly the whole household having been overturned and total destruction having happened, was he thrown into confusion and did he show up (disgrace) his own manliness. Let the rich hear, let the poor hear; for to both the narrative is useful, and to all people the history is profitable, both to those in good days and those in calamities. For having handled both weapons the contender of piety, the crowned one of the inhabited world, set up the trophy in both; and that demon having come against him toward every form of war, he drew up against all, and in all was proclaimed. And just as a noble soldier, knowing to fight by night, to fight at walls, to fight on foot, to fight at sea, and to shoot with the bow, and to shake the spear, and with slings and javelins and in every manner of battle to prevail over the enemies and everywhere to conquer; so then that noble man too bore every trial with much courage, the one from poverty, the one from famine, the one from disease, the one from pain, the one from loss of children, the one from the friends, the one from the enemies, the one from the wife, the one from the household servants. For there was not a human calamity which was not emptied out into the body of that man. But nevertheless he was carried over all the nets, and became higher than the reeds of the devil. And the more wonderful thing, that both all things to him, and all things with excess, and all things at one time. For do not see this, that he suffered so many things; but add that it was not little by little, nor from an interval, but at one time and together. And this is no small addition of trials. For of the other people, each, first, no one would be found having endured all things together; but if he wrestles with poverty, nevertheless he enjoys health; and if he was pierced around by poverty and disease, yet often he enjoyed a wife consoling the terrible things and becoming to him instead of a harbour. And if he did not enjoy such a wife, yet not one counselled so destructively; yet he did not also lose the children all at once; and if also at once, yet not by such a manner of end; and if also by such a manner of end, yet he had friends comforting; and if he did not have comforting ones, yet not also ones so trampling on him; and if also trampling, yet not also household servants reproaching; and if also reproaching, yet not also spitting into his face; and if also spitting into the face, yet he was not also pierced round by such a disease, but enjoyed a room and a shelter, and was not sitting on the dung heap; and if he was also sitting on the dung heap, yet he had those stretching out a hand; and if he did not have those stretching out a hand, yet not also ones trampling on him. But this one bore all these things. Verse 11. They came each from his own country to him, Eliphaz the king of the Temanites, Baldad the tyrant of the Sauchaeans, Sophar king of the Minaeans. Friendly is your presence, friendly the exhortation. Eliphaz: God scattered me, or, the contempt of my God. Teman: their eclipse. Sophar: watcher, or contempt. Baldad: becoming old, and glorious. Sauchaeans: their idle chatter. Verse 11. And having heard, his three friends, all the evil things that had come upon him, came each from his own country to him. pass_b_english: … recounted, and then she brings in her shameless counsel. And she does not even say to him openly, “Blaspheme.” For those who give wicked counsel do not dare to bring their counsel in uncovered. What are you saying, woman? When you ought to appease him, when you ought to reconcile him, do you advise him rather to provoke him? For if God did these things, one must entreat him, not blaspheme him. And how is it plain that I shall die even [if I speak]? But see what the woman thought about blasphemy: she supposed it able to bring death on the spot.

“If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear the evil?” (Job 2:10). For this blessed man, struck from every side, stood all the more firmly, and though he took countless arrows, he did not give way. He emptied the devil's quiver, but he himself did not fall, nor was he tripped up. Like the best of pilots, he was neither sunk when the sea raged and the waves rose up, nor did he grow careless when it was calm; in both kinds of season alike he kept his skill the same. Wealth did not puff him up, nor did poverty humble him. When affairs ran with the current, he did not lie back at his ease; and when nearly his whole household was overturned and utter ruin came, he was not thrown into confusion and did not disgrace his own courage.

Let the rich listen, let the poor listen. The account is useful to both, and the story profits everyone, those who prosper and those in calamity. For the champion of godliness, the crowned victor of the whole world, handled both kinds of weapons and set up his trophy in both; and when that demon came at him with every kind of warfare, he drew up his line against all of it and was proclaimed victor in all. Like a noble soldier who knows how to fight by night, to fight at walls, on foot and at sea, to shoot the bow and brandish the spear, and with slings and javelins and every manner of battle to overcome the enemy and win everywhere, so that noble man bore every trial with great courage: the trial from poverty, from hunger, from disease, from pain, from the loss of his children, from his friends, from his enemies, from his wife, from his servants. There was no human calamity that was not poured out on his body. Yet he rose above all the nets and climbed higher than the devil's fowling reeds.

And what is more wonderful still: everything came on him, everything beyond measure, and everything at once. Do not look only at this, that he suffered so much; add that it came not little by little, nor at intervals, but all together and at once. And this is no small addition to the trials. Among other men, first of all, no one would be found who has endured everything together. If a man wrestles with poverty, he still enjoys health. If he has been pierced through by poverty and disease both, he has often had a wife to console him in his troubles and to be a harbour for him. If he did not have such a wife, at least he had not been given such ruinous advice. If he had, at least he did not lose all his children at once. If he did lose them at once, at least not by such a kind of death. If even by such a death, still he had friends to comfort him. If he had none to comfort him, at least none trampled on him like this. If they did trample on him, at least his servants did not reproach him. If they reproached him, at least they did not spit in his face. If they spat in his face, at least he was not pierced through by such a disease, but had a room and a roof, and did not sit on the dung heap. If he did sit on the dung heap, at least he had people to hold out a hand to him. If he had no one to hold out a hand, at least he had no one trampling on him. But this man endured all of it.

“They came to him, each from his own country: Eliphaz king of the Temanites, Baldad sovereign of the Sauchaeans, Sophar king of the Minaeans” (Job 2:11). Your presence is friendly, and friendly is the advice. Eliphaz: “God has scattered me,” or “contempt of my God.” Teman: “their failing.” Sophar: “watchman,” or “contempt.” Baldad: “growing old,” and “glorious.” Sauchaeans: “their idle talk.”

“When his three friends heard of all the evils that had come upon him, they came to him, each from his own country” (Job 2:11).
